{{Short description|Combination of higher category theory with Chern–Weil theory}}
In [[mathematics]], '''∞-Chern–Weil theory''' is a generalized formulation of [[Chern–Weil theory]] from [[differential geometry]] using the formalism of [[higher category theory]]. The theory is named after [[Shiing-Shen Chern]] and [[André Weil]], who first constructed the [[Chern–Weil homomorphism]] in the 1940s, although the generalization was not developed by them.

== Generalization ==
There are three equivalent ways to describe the <math>k</math>-th [[Chern class]] of complex [[vector bundle]]s of rank <math>n</math>, which is as a:

* (1-categorical) [[natural transformation]] <math>[-,\operatorname{BU}(n)]\Rightarrow[-,K(\mathbb{Z},2k)]</math>
* [[homotopy class]] of a [[continuous map]] <math>\operatorname{BU}(n)\rightarrow K(\mathbb{Z},2k)</math>
* [[singular cohomology]] class in <math>H^{2k}(\operatorname{BU}(n),\mathbb{Z})</math>

<math>\operatorname{BU}(n)</math> is the [[Classifying space for U(n)|classifying space]] for the [[unitary group]] <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> and <math>K(\mathbb{Z},2k)</math> is an [[Eilenberg–MacLane space]], which [[Representable functor|represent]] the set of complex [[vector bundle]]s of rank <math>n</math> with <math>[-,\operatorname{BU}(n)]\cong\operatorname{Vect}_\mathbb{C}^n(-)</math> and singular cohomology with <math>[-,K(\mathbb{Z},2k)]
\cong H^{2k}(-,\mathbb{Z})</math>. The equivalence between the former two descriptions is given by the [[Yoneda lemma]]. The equivalence between the latter two descriptions is given again by the classification of singular cohomology by Eilenberg–MacLane spaces. The singular cohomology class corresponding to the Chern class is that of the [[universal vector bundle]], hence <math>c_k(\gamma_\mathbb{C}^n)
\in H^{2k}(\operatorname{BU}(n),\mathbb{Z})</math>.

A simple example motivating the necessity for a wider view and the description by higher structures is the classifying space <math>\operatorname{BU}(1)
\cong\mathbb{C}P^\infty</math>. It has a [[H-space]] structure, which is unique up to homotopy, so one can again consider its classifying space, which is denoted <math>\operatorname{B^2U}(1)</math>. Due to this property, <math>\operatorname{U}(1)
\cong S^1</math>is a [[2-group]] and <math>\operatorname{B^2U}(1)</math> is a Lie 2-groupoid.<ref>Schreiber 2013, 1.2.6.2 on p. 102</ref> Going to the classifying space shifts the homotopy group up, hence <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>, <math>\operatorname{BU}(1)</math> and <math>\operatorname{B^2U}(1)</math> are the Eilenberg–MacLane spaces <math>K(\mathbb{Z},1)</math>, <math>K(\mathbb{Z},2)</math> and <math>K(\mathbb{Z},3)</math> respectively. Describing the Eilenberg–MacLane space <math>K(\mathbb{Z},2k)</math> therefore requires repeating this process, for which switching to ∞-groups is necessary. Since [[loop space]]s shift the homotopy group down, the classifying space in the ∞-category <math>\operatorname{Top}</math> of topological spaces is in general known as ''delooping''. In the [[∞-topos]] <math>\infty\operatorname{Grpd}</math> of ∞-groupoids, it corresponds to forming the ∞-category with a single object.

== ∞-Chern–Weil homomorphism ==
Let <math>\mathbf{H}</math> be a ∞-topos. The [[fundamental ∞-groupoid]] <math>\Pi\colon\mathbf{H}\rightarrow\infty\operatorname{Grpd}</math> has a right adjoint <math>\operatorname{Disc}\colon
\infty\operatorname{Grpd}\rightarrow\mathbf{H}</math>, which again has a right adjoint <math>\Gamma\colon
\mathbf{H}\rightarrow\infty\operatorname{Grpd}</math>, so <math>\Pi\dashv\operatorname{Disc}\dashv\Gamma</math>.<ref>Schreiber 2013, p. 97</ref> Let <math>\textstyle\int
:=\operatorname{Disc}\circ\Pi\colon
\mathbf{H}\rightarrow\mathbf{H}</math> and <math>\flat
:=\operatorname{Disc}\circ\Gamma\colon
\mathbf{H}\rightarrow\mathbf{H}</math>, then there is an adjunction <math>\textstyle\int\dashv\flat</math>.<ref name=":0">Schreiber 2013,  1.2.7.2 on p. 134-136</ref>

Let <math>G</math> be an ∞-group and <math>\mathbf{B}G</math> its delooping. A characteristic class is a morphism <math>c\colon
\mathbf{B}G\rightarrow\mathbf{B}^n\operatorname{U}(1)</math>. The [[Counit (category theory)|counit]] of <math>\operatorname{Disc}\dashv\Gamma</math> provides a canonical map  <math>\flat\mathbf{B}G\rightarrow\mathbf{B}G</math>. Its [[homotopy fiber]], which gives the obstruction to the existence of flat lifts, is denoted <math>\flat_\mathrm{dR}\mathbf{B}G</math> (with dR standing for [[Georges de Rham|de Rham]]), so there is a sequence <math>\flat_\mathrm{dR}\mathbf{B}G\rightarrow\flat\mathbf{B}G\rightarrow\mathbf{B}G</math>. In case of <math>G=\mathbf{B}^{n-1}\operatorname{U}(1)</math>, there is also a connecting morphism <math>\operatorname{curv}\colon\mathbf{B}^n\operatorname{U}(1)\rightarrow\flat_\mathrm{dR}\mathbf{B}^{n+1}\operatorname{U}(1)</math> called curvature, which extends the sequence and even connects all of them into a single long sequence. For an ∞-group <math>G</math>, the composition:

: <math>\operatorname{curv}\circ c\colon
\mathbf{B}G\rightarrow\flat_\mathrm{dR}\mathbf{B}^{n+1}\operatorname{U}(1)</math>

is the ''∞-Chern–Weil homomorphism''.<ref name=":0" /> Through [[Function composition|postcomposition]], it assigns a <math>G</math>-principal ∞-bundle <math>X\rightarrow\mathbf{B}G</math> a [[de Rham cohomology]] class <math>X\rightarrow\flat_\mathrm{dR}\mathbf{B}^{n+1}\operatorname{U}(1)</math>, alternatively written as a morphism <math>H(X,G)\rightarrow H_\mathrm{dR}^{n+1}(X)</math> with intrinsic<ref>Schreiber 2013, p. 96</ref> and de Rham cohomology:

: <math>H(X,G)
:=\pi_0\mathbf{H}(X,\mathbf{B}G);</math>
: <math>H_\mathrm{dR}^n(X,G)
:=\pi_0\mathbf{H}(X,\flat_\mathrm{dR}\mathbf{B}G).</math>

Additionally, there is also flat differential <math>G</math>-valued cohomology:

: <math>H_\mathrm{flat}(X,G)
:=\pi_0\mathbf{H}(X,\flat\mathbf{B}G)
\cong\pi_0\mathbf{H}(\textstyle\int X,\mathbf{B}G)
=H(\textstyle\int X,G)</math>

with the canonical morphism <math>\flat\mathbf{B}G\rightarrow\mathbf{B}G</math> inducing a [[Forgetful functor|forgetful]] morphism <math>H_\mathrm{flat}(X,G)\rightarrow H(X,G)</math>.<ref name=":0" />
